title: August 2016 (Paper II - Re-Exam)
subtitle: Verified Answer Key (50/50 Qs) + Crisp Simple-English Explanations

items.title: Q1 · August 2016 (Paper II - Re-Exam)
items.meta: Victorian Period · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story
items.stem: What is the fate of ignorance in Bunyan’s Pilgrim’s Progress?
options: He drowns in the River of Death
He discovers the way to Hell
items.explanation: In John Bunyan's The Pilgrim's Progress (1678), Ignorance is ferried across the River of Death by Vain-Hope, but because he lacks a certificate of entry at the Celestial City, two Shining Ones bind him and cast him into the door on the side of the hill leading to Hell. This prompts the concluding reflection that there is a way to Hell even from the gates of Heaven.

items.title: Q2 · August 2016 (Paper II - Re-Exam)
items.meta: Modernist & Early 20th Century · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose
items.stem: God is referred to as “The President of Immortals” in
items.explanation: In the final chapter of Thomas Hardy's novel Tess of the d'Urbervilles (1891), Hardy concludes Tess's tragic execution with the famous line: "'Justice' was done, and the President of the Immortals, in Aeschylean phrase, had ended his sport with Tess."

items.title: Q3 · August 2016 (Paper II - Re-Exam)
items.meta: Romantic Period · Unit II: Poetry
items.stem: Match the character with the author : List – I I. Madeline II. Prometheus III. Urizen IV. Childe Harold List – II A. Blake B. Byron C. Shelley D. Keats
items.explanation: The correct pairings are: Madeline appears in John Keats's narrative poem The Eve of St. Agnes (1820) [I-D]; Prometheus is the suffering hero of Percy Bysshe Shelley's lyrical drama Prometheus Unbound (1820) [II-C]; Urizen is the embodiment of conventional reason and law in William Blake's The Book of Urizen (1794) [III-A]; and Childe Harold is the autobiographical wanderer in Lord Byron's Childe Harold's Pilgrimage (1812–1818) [IV-B].

items.title: Q4 · August 2016 (Paper II - Re-Exam)
items.meta: Modernist & Early 20th Century · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose
items.stem: The phrase “loud colour” is an example of
items.explanation: Synaesthesia is a rhetorical figure and sensory crossover in which one sense modality is described in terms of another, as in describing visual appearance through auditory perception in "loud colour."

items.title: Q5 · August 2016 (Paper II - Re-Exam)
items.meta: Renaissance, Elizabethan & Jacobean Age · Unit I: Drama
items.stem: In one of Marlowe’s plays the hero is warned not “to practise more than heavenly power permits.” Identify the play.
items.explanation: In Christopher Marlowe's tragedy Doctor Faustus (c. 1592), the Chorus delivers the final moral epilogue warning the audience "Only to wonder at unlawful things, / Whose deepness doth entice such forward wits / To practise more than heavenly power permits."

items.title: Q6 · August 2016 (Paper II - Re-Exam)
items.meta: Victorian Period · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story
items.stem: Match the Graham Greene novel with its setting : List – I I. The Ministry of Fear II. The Third Man III. The Power and the Glory IV. The Quiet American List – II A. Vienna B. Mexico C. Vietnam D. London
items.explanation: The correct novel settings for Graham Greene are: The Ministry of Fear (1943) takes place in Blitz-era London [I-D]; The Third Man (1950) is set in postwar divided Vienna [II-A]; The Power and the Glory (1940) portrays religious persecution in 1930s Mexico [III-B]; and The Quiet American (1955) is set in Saigon during the First Indochina War in Vietnam [IV-C].

items.title: Q7 · August 2016 (Paper II - Re-Exam)
items.meta: Victorian Period · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story
items.stem: What was the title of the collection of short stories published by James Joyce in 1914?
items.explanation: James Joyce published Dubliners in 1914, a landmark collection of fifteen realist short stories chronicling paralysis and moments of epiphany across childhood, adolescence, mature life, and public life in Dublin.

items.title: Q8 · August 2016 (Paper II - Re-Exam)
items.meta: Victorian Period · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story
items.stem: Patrick White’s classic work Voss is based on the story of a …………… explorer.
items.explanation: Patrick White's 1957 classic novel Voss is based on the historic 1848 inland Australian expedition led by the German explorer and naturalist Ludwig Leichhardt.

items.title: Q9 · August 2016 (Paper II - Re-Exam)
items.meta: Literary Criticism & Theory · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem: In “Tradition and Individual Talent” Eliot describes the workings of the poet’s mind in terms of which of the following?
items.explanation: In his 1919 critical essay "Tradition and Individual Talent", T.S. Eliot compares the poet's mind to a catalyst in a chemical reaction, specifically a shred of platinum that causes sulphur dioxide and oxygen to form sulphurous acid while remaining completely unaffected itself.

items.title: Q10 · August 2016 (Paper II - Re-Exam)
items.meta: Renaissance, Elizabethan & Jacobean Age · Unit I: Drama
items.stem: Who among the following wrote an immensely powerful play about the remapping of Irish places with new British names?
items.explanation: Irish dramatist Brian Friel wrote Translations (1980), set in 1833 in the Donegal town of Baile Beag (Ballybeg), which depicts the British Army's Ordnance Survey replacing Gaelic place names with standardized English versions.

items.title: Q11 · August 2016 (Paper II - Re-Exam)
items.meta: Modernist & Early 20th Century · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose
items.stem: Identify the term among the following which does not relate to a movement in art or literature.
items.explanation: Empiricism is a philosophical epistemological theory associated with Locke, Berkeley, and Hume asserting that knowledge derives from sensory experience, whereas Cubism, Expressionism, and Surrealism are prominent artistic and literary movements of the early twentieth century.

items.title: Q12 · August 2016 (Paper II - Re-Exam)
items.meta: Literary Criticism & Theory · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem: “Kubla Khan” is thought to have been written in 1797, but it was not published until 1816. Who persuaded Coleridge to publish it?
items.explanation: Samuel Taylor Coleridge composed "Kubla Khan" in 1797 following an opium-influenced dream, but kept it unpublished until Lord Byron heard Coleridge recite it in 1816 and persuaded him to publish it with John Murray.

items.title: Q13 · August 2016 (Paper II - Re-Exam)
items.meta: Literary Criticism & Theory · Unit IX: Literary Theory Post World War II
items.stem: In Restoration comedy, character names often reveal character traits. What trait does the name Sir Wilfull Witwoud reveal?
options: A desire to be thought of as witty
items.explanation: In Restoration comedy, "Witwoud" is a charactonym meaning "wit-would"—someone who desperately desires and tries to appear witty but lacks genuine wit, exemplified by Sir Wilfull Witwoud and his half-brother in William Congreve's The Way of the World (1700).

items.title: Q14 · August 2016 (Paper II - Re-Exam)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit V: Language: Basic Concepts, Theories and Pedagogy
items.stem: From the following list identify the two novels published by John Henry Newman I. The Grammar of Assent II. Apologia pro vita sua III. Loss and Gain IV. Callista The right combination according to the code is :
items.explanation: John Henry Newman published two novels: Loss and Gain (1848), which dramatizes an Oxford student's conversion to Roman Catholicism, and Callista (1855), set in third-century Christian Africa. Statements I (An Essay in Aid of a Grammar of Assent, 1870) and II (Apologia Pro Vita Sua, 1864) are philosophical and autobiographical works rather than novels.

items.title: Q15 · August 2016 (Paper II - Re-Exam)
items.meta: Romantic Period · Unit II: Poetry
items.stem: Consider the following lines from Beowulf : What literary device does the poet use in these lines? A few miles from here a frost-stiffened wood waits and keeps watch above a mere.
items.explanation: In the Old English epic Beowulf, the line "a frost-stiffened wood waits and keeps watch above a mere" uses personification by giving inanimate trees human consciousness and vigilance.

items.title: Q16 · August 2016 (Paper II - Re-Exam)
items.meta: Renaissance, Elizabethan & Jacobean Age · Unit I: Drama
items.stem: Which of the following plays of Bernard Shaw attacks Darwinism?
items.explanation: In Back to Methuselah (1921), a five-part play cycle spanning from the Garden of Eden into the distant future, George Bernard Shaw explicitly attacks Darwinian natural selection as blind and mechanistic, championing Lamarckian creative evolution driven by the Life Force.

items.title: Q17 · August 2016 (Paper II - Re-Exam)
items.meta: Modernist & Early 20th Century · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose
items.stem: In King Lear to which woman has Edmund sworn his love?
items.explanation: In Shakespeare's King Lear (c. 1606), the treacherous Edmund duplicitously woos both of Lear's elder daughters, declaring in Act 5, Scene 1: "To both these sisters have I sworn my love; / Each jealous of the other, as the stung / Are of the adder."

items.title: Q18 · August 2016 (Paper II - Re-Exam)
items.meta: Romantic Period · Unit II: Poetry
items.stem: The poetic line, “Break, break, break” is an example of
items.explanation: In Alfred, Lord Tennyson's 1842 lyric "Break, Break, Break", the opening three monosyllabic words are each heavily stressed, creating successive spondees that evoke the relentless, rhythmic pounding of the sea against the shore.

items.title: Q19 · August 2016 (Paper II - Re-Exam)
items.meta: Renaissance, Elizabethan & Jacobean Age · Unit I: Drama
items.stem: Ben Jonson’s Pleasure Reconciled to Virtue is a
items.explanation: Pleasure Reconciled to Virtue (1618) is a Stuart court masque written by Ben Jonson and designed by Inigo Jones, which famously featured Prince Charles dancing in his first court performance.

items.title: Q20 · August 2016 (Paper II - Re-Exam)
items.meta: Renaissance, Elizabethan & Jacobean Age · Unit I: Drama
items.stem: What is the rhyme scheme of the Shakespearean sonnet?
options: aa bb cc dd aa bb dd
items.explanation: The Shakespearean (English) sonnet consists of fourteen lines of iambic pentameter arranged into three quatrains and a concluding rhyming couplet, following the rhyme scheme abab cdcd efef gg.

items.title: Q21 · August 2016 (Paper II - Re-Exam)
items.meta: Modernist & Early 20th Century · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose
items.stem: In More’s Utopia what religion is practised by the Utopians?
options: Belief in a single, infinite power and sun, moon and planetary worship
items.explanation: In Book II of Thomas More's Utopia (1516), the Utopians enjoy religious freedom: while some venerate heavenly bodies like the sun, moon, or planets, the vast majority believe in a single, unsearchable, infinite divine presence named Mythras.

items.title: Q22 · August 2016 (Paper II - Re-Exam)
items.meta: Literary Criticism & Theory · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem: In Book 5 of prelude, Wordsworth dreams of an Arab in the desert after reading which great work?
items.explanation: In Book 5 ("Books") of William Wordsworth's The Prelude (1805/1850), the speaker falls asleep while reading Miguel de Cervantes's Don Quixote and dreams of an Arab phantom on a camel carrying a stone (geometry) and a shell (poetry).

items.title: Q23 · August 2016 (Paper II - Re-Exam)
items.meta: Victorian Period · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story
items.stem: Lady Dedlock is a character in Dickens’s
items.explanation: Lady Honoria Dedlock is the aristocratic protagonist of Charles Dickens's Bleak House (1852–1853), whose concealed romance with Captain Hawdon and illegitimate daughter Esther Summerson form the novel's central mystery.

items.title: Q24 · August 2016 (Paper II - Re-Exam)
items.meta: Romantic Period · Unit II: Poetry
items.stem: Which of Keats's poems was originally intended to be part of a collection of verse-tales based on stories by Boccaccio?
items.explanation: John Keats's narrative poem Isabella; or, The Pot of Basil (1818, published 1820) adapts a tale from Giovanni Boccaccio's Decameron (Day IV, Story 5) and was originally intended for a collaborative volume of versified Boccaccio stories with John Hamilton Reynolds.

items.title: Q25 · August 2016 (Paper II - Re-Exam)
items.meta: Modernist & Early 20th Century · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose
items.stem: Where does Conrad’s Heart of Darkness begin?
items.explanation: Joseph Conrad's Heart of Darkness (1899) begins aboard the cruising yawl Nellie anchored on the River Thames at Gravesend, where Marlow begins narrating his voyage into the Belgian Congo to his fellow sailors.

items.title: Q26 · August 2016 (Paper II - Re-Exam)
items.meta: Modernist & Early 20th Century · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose
items.stem: In Gulliver’s Travels which of the following ideas is not a product of the Academy of Lagado?
options: A proposal to end speech altogether, by carrying around sacks of the things that words signify.
A project for truncating words and shortening sentences by leaving out verbs.
A digestible dictionary, written on a water.
items.explanation: In Part III, Chapter 5 of Jonathan Swift's Gulliver's Travels (1726), the Grand Academy of Lagado experiments with an automatic sentence-making engine, carrying physical objects to replace spoken words, and truncating sentences; the ingestible teaching method involves writing mathematical propositions on thin wafers, not a dictionary on water.

items.title: Q27 · August 2016 (Paper II - Re-Exam)
items.meta: Modernist & Early 20th Century · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose
items.stem: Which of the following stories is NOT written by Nathaniel Hawthorne?
items.explanation: "The Purloined Letter" (1844) is Edgar Allan Poe's famous detective story starring C. Auguste Dupin, whereas "The Minister's Black Veil" (1836), "Young Goodman Brown" (1835), and "My Kinsman, Major Molineux" (1832) are all celebrated tales by Nathaniel Hawthorne.

items.title: Q28 · August 2016 (Paper II - Re-Exam)
items.meta: Renaissance, Elizabethan & Jacobean Age · Unit I: Drama
items.stem: What attributes of Shakespeare’s characterization does Johnson admire in his preface to Shakespeare?
options: The way his characters represent particular times and places.
The way his characters exhibit quirks representative of their humours or professions.
The way his characters portray the general passions and principles of human nature.
The way his characters portray real individuals.
items.explanation: In his Preface to Shakespeare (1765), Samuel Johnson lauds Shakespeare as "the poet of nature," emphasizing that his characters do not merely exhibit peculiarities of particular places or professions, but portray the enduring passions and principles of universal human nature.

items.title: Q29 · August 2016 (Paper II - Re-Exam)
items.meta: Literary Criticism & Theory · Unit IX: Literary Theory Post World War II
items.stem: According to Foucault sexuality points to discourses about all the following EXCEPT
items.explanation: In The History of Sexuality, Volume 1 (1976), Michel Foucault analyzes how modern power categorized and regulated sex through the institutional discourses of medicine, psychiatry/psychology, and law/criminology, while anthropology was not one of these key regulatory discourses.

items.title: Q30 · August 2016 (Paper II - Re-Exam)
items.meta: Modernist & Early 20th Century · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose
items.stem: “All Arabia breathes from yonder box.” This line from The Rape of the Lock is an example of
items.explanation: In Alexander Pope's mock-heroic poem The Rape of the Lock (1714, Canto I, line 134), the phrase "All Arabia breathes from yonder box" uses metonymy by naming the country of origin to represent the fragrant perfumes derived from it.

items.title: Q31 · August 2016 (Paper II - Re-Exam)
items.meta: Modernist & Early 20th Century · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose
items.stem: Who among the following addresses the reader in a substantial Preface to Robert Burton’s Anatomy of Melancholy?
items.explanation: Robert Burton introduces his vast encyclopedic treatise The Anatomy of Melancholy (1621) with a substantial satirical preface titled "Democritus Junior to the Reader", adopting the persona of the Greek laughing philosopher Democritus to diagnose human folly.

items.title: Q32 · August 2016 (Paper II - Re-Exam)
items.meta: Modernist & Early 20th Century · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose
items.stem: Which of these is the best paraphrase of the line, “the paths of glory lead but to the grave”?
options: Those who seek glory often die in its pursuit.
Everyone dies, even the famous and glorious.
The pursuit of glory is futile.
The pursuit of glory is dangerous.
items.explanation: In Thomas Gray's "Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard" (1751), the line "The paths of glory lead but to the grave" stresses the inescapable reality of mortality, showing that worldly rank, fame, and military glory all end equally in death.

items.title: Q33 · August 2016 (Paper II - Re-Exam)
items.meta: Victorian Period · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story
items.stem: Which novel did James Joyce call “the English Ulysses”?
items.explanation: In a 1911 lecture delivered in Trieste, James Joyce called Daniel Defoe's Robinson Crusoe (1719) "the English Ulysses", praising Crusoe's independence, practical craftsmanship, and perseverance as the prototypical spirit of the British empire.

items.title: Q34 · August 2016 (Paper II - Re-Exam)
items.meta: Victorian Period · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story
items.stem: What narrative perspective does Chaucer employ in the opening of “The General Prologue”?
items.explanation: Geoffrey Chaucer opens "The General Prologue" to The Canterbury Tales (c. 1387) using a first-person narrator ("Chaucer the Pilgrim"), recounting how he lodged at the Tabard Inn in Southwark ready to embark on his pilgrimage to Canterbury.

items.title: Q35 · August 2016 (Paper II - Re-Exam)
items.meta: Literary Criticism & Theory · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem: A fragmentary unfinished novel entitled Emma was published in Cornhill Magazine. Identify the author.
items.explanation: Charlotte Brontë's unfinished novel fragment Emma, consisting of two completed chapters, was published posthumously in the Cornhill Magazine in April 1860 with an affectionate introductory tribute by William Makepeace Thackeray.

items.title: Q36 · August 2016 (Paper II - Re-Exam)
items.meta: Literary Criticism & Theory · Unit IX: Literary Theory Post World War II
items.stem: The pre-eminent evaluative criterion of F.R. Leavis’s Great Tradition is
items.explanation: In The Great Tradition (1948), critic F.R. Leavis identifies a profound, mature "moral interest in life" as the central criterion that distinguishes the supreme English novelists—Jane Austen, George Eliot, Henry James, and Joseph Conrad.

items.title: Q37 · August 2016 (Paper II - Re-Exam)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit V: Language: Basic Concepts, Theories and Pedagogy
items.stem: In Wide Sargasso Sea what is the name of Rochester’s Creole wife-to-be?
items.explanation: In Jean Rhys's Wide Sargasso Sea (1966), the Jamaican Creole heiress Antoinette Cosway is renamed "Bertha" by her English husband Rochester, who imposes this name upon her as he strips her of her identity and brings her to England as the madwoman in Charlotte Brontë's Jane Eyre.

items.title: Q38 · August 2016 (Paper II - Re-Exam)
items.meta: Romantic Period · Unit II: Poetry
items.stem: Which popular nursery rhyme is mentioned at the end of The Waste land?
items.explanation: In the final section ("What the Thunder Said") of T.S. Eliot's The Waste Land (1922), line 426 quotes the traditional nursery rhyme: "London Bridge is falling down falling down falling down."

items.title: Q39 · August 2016 (Paper II - Re-Exam)
items.meta: Modernist & Early 20th Century · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose
items.stem: Purple Hibiscus is a work by
items.explanation: Purple Hibiscus (2003) is the acclaimed debut novel of Nigerian author Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie, narrated by fifteen-year-old Kambili Achike as she navigates her wealthy, religiously authoritarian household in post-coup Nigeria.

items.title: Q40 · August 2016 (Paper II - Re-Exam)
items.meta: Modernist & Early 20th Century · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose
items.stem: Which country is Jacques Derrida born in?
items.explanation: French philosopher Jacques Derrida was born in 1930 in El Biar, French Algeria, into an Algerian Sephardic Jewish family, before moving to Paris in 1949 to pursue his advanced philosophical studies.

items.title: Q41 · August 2016 (Paper II - Re-Exam)
items.meta: Literary Criticism & Theory · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem: Which of the following plays is NOT part of the so-called Arnold Wesker Trilogy?
items.explanation: The Arnold Wesker Trilogy consists of Chicken Soup with Barley (1958), Roots (1959), and I'm Talking about Jerusalem (1960). Chips with Everything (1962) is a separate, standalone play by Wesker about class conflict and rebellion within a Royal Air Force recruit camp.

items.title: Q42 · August 2016 (Paper II - Re-Exam)
items.meta: Renaissance, Elizabethan & Jacobean Age · Unit I: Drama
items.stem: Identify the play from among the following in which a spendthrift young man auctions away the portraits of his ancestors :
items.explanation: In Richard Brinsley Sheridan's comedy of manners The School for Scandal (1777, Act IV, Scene 1), the good-natured spendthrift Charles Surface auctions off his ancestors' family portraits to his disguised uncle Oliver, refusing only to sell Oliver's own picture.

items.title: Q43 · August 2016 (Paper II - Re-Exam)
items.meta: Modernist & Early 20th Century · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose
items.stem: Which of the following is NOT written by Rudyard Kipling?
items.explanation: The Secret Garden (1911) was written by Frances Hodgson Burnett, whereas Just So Stories (1902), Puck of Pook's Hill (1906), and Rewards and Fairies (1910) are all classic children's collections by Rudyard Kipling.

items.title: Q44 · August 2016 (Paper II - Re-Exam)
items.meta: Modernist & Early 20th Century · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose
items.stem: In Faerie Queene what is Redcrosse’s reward for slaying the Dragon?
options: The satisfaction of accomplishing the end of a righteous quest
Una’s hand in marriage and her parents’ kingdom
items.explanation: In Book I, Canto XII of Edmund Spenser's The Faerie Queene (1590), after slaying the dragon that besieged the kingdom of Eden, the Redcrosse Knight is rewarded with Princess Una's hand in marriage and heirship to her parents' kingdom.

items.title: Q45 · August 2016 (Paper II - Re-Exam)
items.meta: Victorian Period · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story
items.stem: Which of the following novels has the death of General Muhammad Zia ul-Haq, the former President of Pakistan, at its centre?
items.explanation: Mohammed Hanif's satirical political novel A Case of Exploding Mangoes (2008) centers on the mysterious August 1988 plane crash that killed Pakistan's military president, General Muhammad Zia-ul-Haq.

items.title: Q46 · August 2016 (Paper II - Re-Exam)
items.meta: Modernist & Early 20th Century · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose
items.stem: Lewis Carroll is a pseudonym that refers to
items.explanation: Lewis Carroll was the pen name of Charles Lutwidge Dodgson (1832–1898), an Oxford mathematician and logician famed for writing Alice's Adventures in Wonderland (1865) and Through the Looking-Glass (1871).

items.title: Q47 · August 2016 (Paper II - Re-Exam)
items.meta: Romantic Period · Unit II: Poetry
items.stem: One of the following collections initiated confessional poetry in America, a new mode in which the poet bared his/her most tormenting personal problems with great honesty and intensity.
items.explanation: Robert Lowell's 1959 collection Life Studies launched the confessional poetry movement in American literature, pioneering candid autobiographical verse detailing personal breakdown, family conflict, and psychiatric hospitalization.

items.title: Q48 · August 2016 (Paper II - Re-Exam)
items.meta: Renaissance, Elizabethan & Jacobean Age · Unit I: Drama
items.stem: The Marriage of Heaven and Hell is a …………… by …………….
items.explanation: The Marriage of Heaven and Hell (1790–1793) is an illustrated prophetic prose-and-verse poem by William Blake that satirizes conventional moral orthodoxy and Emanuel Swedenborg's theology through the "Proverbs of Hell."

items.title: Q49 · August 2016 (Paper II - Re-Exam)
items.meta: Romantic Period · Unit II: Poetry
items.stem: In the poem or invocation at the opening of Book 3, Paradise Lost, Milton asks for divine help in writing his epic. He states that he is in particular need of aid because he has what he considers to be a disability. What is it?
items.explanation: In the opening invocation to Book 3 of Paradise Lost (1667), John Milton laments his total blindness, which struck him in 1652, and prays for divine internal illumination so that he may see and declare things invisible to mortal sight.

items.title: Q50 · August 2016 (Paper II - Re-Exam)
items.meta: Romantic Period · Unit II: Poetry
items.stem: Match the poets with the collection : List – I I. Philip Larkin II. Geoffrey Hill III. Ted Hughes IV. Seamus Heaney List – II A. Lupercal B. Door into the Dark C. The Less Deceived D. For the Unfallen
items.explanation: The correct poetic collections and authors are: Philip Larkin published The Less Deceived in 1955 [I-C]; Geoffrey Hill debuted with For the Unfallen in 1959 [II-D]; Ted Hughes published his acclaimed collection Lupercal in 1960 [III-A]; and Seamus Heaney published Door into the Dark in 1969 [IV-B].
